name: Drafting Proposals from Past Work
title: Drafting Proposals from Past Work
answer: Drafting proposals from past work means reusing material a researcher has already written, such as prior grant narratives, progress reports, methods sections, and published papers, as the starting point for a new funding application. It covers the whole document, not just the science: the aims page, the background, the approach, the budget justification, and the biosketch all draw on text that already exists somewhere. The task is less about writing from nothing and more about selecting, cutting, and reshaping old prose so it answers the specific call in front of you. A proposal for a different funder, a different panel, or a different scope usually needs the same facts told in a new order and a new voice.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Drafting proposals from past work means reusing material a researcher has already written, such as prior grant narratives, progress reports, methods sections, and published papers, as the starting point for a new funding application. sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The raw material lives in reference managers, institutional repositories, old submission portals, and personal folders of Word files and PDFs. Most researchers work in a word processor, with Zotero, EndNote, or Mendeley holding the citations and a shared drive or cloud folder holding the drafts. Funding agencies impose their own formats, page limits, and submission systems, so the same content often has to be reflowed into a sponsor template before it can be sent. Where a lab has a writing group or a grants office, that office usually keeps the boilerplate, the institutional language, and the past award records that get reused.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The practical work starts with a close reading of the new call, then a search through past documents for passages that still fit. Researchers copy paragraphs into a fresh file, strip out references to the old project, and rewrite the framing so the aims match the new solicitation. Large language models are now used to summarize old narratives, suggest rephrasings, or draft a first pass at a section, but the researcher still checks every claim, number, and citation against the source. Reviewers and program officers read for fit and feasibility, so the reused text has to be re-argued rather than pasted. Version control matters, because a paragraph lifted from a three year old proposal may describe methods the lab no longer uses.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Reusing your own text raises questions of self plagiarism, and many funders and journals treat overlapping text as a disclosure issue rather than a private matter. Prior work must be cited, preliminary results must be attributed correctly, and any text written by a coauthor or a grant writer needs that person's agreement before it is reused. Institutional review, conflict of interest rules, and sponsor policies on overlapping submissions all apply, and some agencies require a statement about prior or pending support. If a language model helped produce text, the researcher remains responsible for its accuracy and for any fabricated citation or result. Nothing here is legal advice, and specific rules vary by funder and institution.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Tooling is moving toward searchable personal libraries that can retrieve a relevant passage from years of past writing and adapt it to a new call, with the researcher editing rather than composing from scratch. Funders are also tightening rules on text overlap and on the use of generative tools in applications, so the value shifts from producing words to documenting where they came from. The likely result is that proposal writing becomes more like curation and less like blank page drafting, with provenance and disclosure built into the workflow. Researchers who keep clean, well tagged records of past work will find the reuse easier and the compliance questions simpler.
